Note · Pfeffer — Power

4 min read1,003 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-pfeffer-power.md

Canon · Cluster: Power & Organizational Politics · Maps to Course 09 (Leadership & OB), E1 (Leading at Scale)

  • Source: Jeffrey Pfeffer, Power: Why Some People Have It — and Others Don't (2010)
  • Core claim: Organizational power doesn't come from being right. It comes from controlling resources, building alliances, managing information, and understanding who actually decides. People who ignore power dynamics don't transcend them — they just lose to people who don't.
  • Framework:
  • Sources of power: control of resources, position in the information/communication network, alliances, reputation, and personal qualities (will, energy, focus, ambition, political skill).
  • Build power deliberately: get into a department/role near the power, build a personal brand, network before you need it, ask for things, and don't wait to be recognized on merit.
  • Performance ≠ advancement; visibility + relationships with decision-makers often matter more.
  • Applies when: you need to get things done in any real organization — Pfeffer's uncomfortable honesty is that political skill is a prerequisite, not a dirty word.
  • Breaks when: the playbook can curdle into pure careerism that erodes trust and, at scale, the org itself — power acquired is not the same as power deployed well (the values question Pfeffer brackets out). It also reads as cynical-by-design; in genuinely high-trust, mission-driven teams, naked power-seeking backfires and Carnegie's "make others feel valued" (canon carnegie win friends) outperforms. And Munger's lens applies: understand the incentives before you assume someone's power play is what it looks like (canon munger poor charlies almanack).

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-06 — Stanford GSB Pfeffer "Power" book talk, youtube.com/watch?v=0eFln_mdXGY) Pfeffer's own framing is blunter than the book's tidy summary: "the biggest barrier I think for us having power is of course ourselves — we are often times not willing to do what it takes or to make the tradeoffs required to have power." He names the specific self-defeats: we "worry excessively about what others, particularly peers, think" — yet "your direct hierarchical peers are also your competitors" under any up-or-out. And the deepest trap is the just-world reflex: students tell him "these people will get it in the end, so I don't have anything to learn from them," and he counters that "because we believe in a just world we often times don't pay attention to the more interesting people in the organization," leaving us "less vigilant and strategic than required." The cynical extreme is Greene (canon greene 48 laws of power) — whose own summary admits "a lot of it's about defense… knowing that there are malevolent, aggressive, toxic people out there."

  • Researched layer (updated 2026-06-06)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Pfeffer's core mechanism is that power is learnable and earned, not deserved — and that most people refuse to learn it because it offends their sense of fairness. The first practical move is diagnostic: "diagnose who has power — not just the formal power but the informal power; oftentimes it's an assistant or a secretary or people who… aren't that high up in the organization chart" — then "figure out how to get closer to the people with power and get those people on their side" (Stanford GSB, "Why Cultivating Power is the Secret to Success"). Power "is in fact all around them, kind of like air and water and gravity." The contrarian career move follows directly: "why would you go to the same firms that hire all of the best and brightest from all the same schools that you're graduating from? Go find the niche" (Stanford GSB, "Power: Why Some People Have It").
  • Real application (mined): the concrete playbook is mundane and tactical — do "small tasks that make those other individuals' lives easier," network and build social relationships, flatter ("one of the best ways to make people think well of themselves is to flatter them"), and find unexploited resources ("organizations have budgets that will permit you to put together a speaker series… dinners or lunches… that put yourself in the center of a series of relationships"). The hardest discipline is reallocating time: "if you spend all your time with your current close friends, how do you ever make new ones?" — the useful contacts are the weak ties who carry "non-redundant information," not the roommates you already ski with.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: Pfeffer is candid that the playbook has a real price. On authenticity he is provocative: "your job as a leader is not to be authentic or genuine… your job is to be true to what the situation requires of you" — you must "sometimes display emotions that you're not really feeling… but it's what success requires" (Stanford GSB, "Why Cultivating Power"). And on the personal cost: "there's an enormous price for having power… most successful people that I know have to work very, very hard," trading the people you want to be with for the people you need to be with. This is exactly the careerism the note's Breaks-when warns about — power acquired is not power deployed well, and the Greene strand shows how fast "take the credit" curdles.
  • Sources in corpus: Stanford Graduate School of Business — "Power: Why Some People Have It and Others Don't" (youtube.com/watch?v=0eFln_mdXGY) · Stanford GSB — "Jeffrey Pfeffer: Why Cultivating Power is the Secret to Success" (youtube.com/watch?v=AozJ4AkgAMw) · Stanford GSB — "'Power' Fireside Chat: Professor Jeff Pfeffer and Dean Jon Levin" (youtube.com/watch?v=QXtVfrzPYqE) · Robert Greene — "The 48 Laws of Power Summarized in Under 8 Minutes" (youtube.com/watch?v=Ke5kFc7U1h8).
